prompt:
Rewrite the following so it is easier to read. Keep every fact and number.

The checkout-redesign flag sat at 5 percent for eleven days because the canary cohort, drawn by hashing user IDs into 10,000 buckets and admitting the lowest 500, overrepresented legacy accounts created before the 2019 schema migration. Those accounts carried null currency fields, and the new payment-form validation layer choked on them, pushing p99 latency from 340 to 910 milliseconds. Dashboards whispered nothing: the error budget alert threshold averaged across all traffic, so a regression confined to one twentieth of users drowned in the healthy ninety-five. Engineers assumed the stall was a capacity question until someone cohort-sliced the traces and found the null-field cluster. The fix was a two-line default, but the lesson was bigger: a ramp is a flashlight, not a floodlight, and it illuminates only whatever population the hash happens to point at.
text:
The checkout-redesign flag stayed at 5 percent for eleven days. The canary cohort was drawn by hashing user IDs into 10,000 buckets and admitting the lowest 500. That cohort had too many legacy accounts, created before the 2019 schema migration. Those accounts had null currency fields, and the new payment-form validation layer failed on them. This pushed p99 latency from 340 to 910 milliseconds.

The dashboards showed nothing wrong. The error budget alert threshold was averaged across all traffic, so a regression affecting one twentieth of users was hidden by the healthy ninety-five. Engineers assumed the stall was a capacity problem, until someone sliced the traces by cohort and found the cluster of null fields.

The fix was a two-line default. The larger lesson is that a gradual ramp only shows you the population the hash happens to select. It does not show you all your users.
